item.title: 16 killed, 32 injured after 7.0-magnitude quake hits China's Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
LHASA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Sixteen people were killed and 32 others injured after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Baqen County of Nagqu City in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. Thursday (Beijing Time), according to the city's emergency management bureau. As of 2:25 a.m. Friday, 11 of the injured were in serious condition while 21 sustained minor injuries. Over 300 houses collapsed. The damage caused by the quake is being further evaluated, and disaster relief work is underway. More than 300 police officers have been dispatched to the epicenter for relief work while the regional fire and rescue corps has mobilized 347 personnel to the affected areas. ■

item.title: From embroidery to tourism, Yunnan turns ethnic traditions into opportunities
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
KUNMING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- On a warm afternoon, 63-year-old Yi woman Pu Lianying sat in a community workshop, embroidering pink peonies onto black velvet and chatting with friends. Occasionally, tourists stopped by to browse embroidered decorations displayed on a table. The workshop is in Lianjiang Community in Eshan Yi Autonomous County, Yuxi City, southwest China's Yunnan Province, where residents of different ethnic groups, including Yi, Hani and Hui, live side by side. In 2021, several old residential compounds were combined into a modern community with improved public spaces and facilities. The local women's federation helped establish a Yi embroidery workshop, giving residents a place to socialize while keeping traditional craftsmanship alive. Yi embroidery, a traditional skill passed down through generations of the Yi ethnic group, is on China's national intangible cultural heritage list. The workshop brings in recognized inheritors to teach residents, who can choose from traditional designs and smaller contemporary products. Last year, Eshan County sold 40,000 Yi embroidery products, generating about 5 million yuan (about 744,000 U.S. dollars) in income for local residents, said Bai Xuemei, head of the county women's federation. "I enjoy coming here to embroider and chat with my friends," Pu said, pointing to a half-finished traditional cloth used by Yi women to carry babies. Last year, she sold 10 pieces, earning 1,600 yuan per piece. The community's efforts to improve residents' lives extend beyond the embroidery workshop. Li Tianrong, a Han official who heads the subdistrict office administering Lianjiang Community, has learned the Yi language to communicate more easily with elderly residents. The community canteen regularly serves braised beef, a favorite among Yi residents, as well as other popular dishes for older people. Revenue from renting out community-owned shops helps subsidize the canteen, where residents can enjoy a hearty meal for just 14 yuan. Older residents receive discounts and can even have meals delivered to their homes. From helping residents preserve traditional crafts to making daily life more convenient, communities across Yunnan are finding various ways to meet local needs and boost livelihoods. Home to 26 ethnic groups, the province is turning traditional skills into specialty products and tourism experiences. In Jinglai Village in Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, near the China-Myanmar border, local residents are working with businesses to bring traditional crafts and arts to a wider audience. One attraction is slow-wheel pottery, a traditional Dai craft on the national intangible cultural heritage list. Unlike modern electric wheels, the hand-operated wheel turns slowly, requiring artisans to shape the clay through repeated tapping and careful adjustment. The finished pottery retains visible layers of clay, giving it a distinctive rustic appearance. "Our pottery-making skills have been passed down through generations. My mother made the pots and jars we used at home," said Yu Xianglun, a Dai inheritor of the craft. "Now that our pottery has a market, the craft will not be lost." Visitors can also try traditional sugar-making by pushing a long bamboo pole around a wooden pivot to squeeze juice from sugarcane. Some are eager to drink the fresh juice before it is boiled down into sugar. Jinglai Village has brought together over 20 traditional artisans who demonstrate more than 10 crafts, including bamboo weaving and traditional liquor brewing. The scenic area provides monthly subsidies of 1,500 to 3,000 yuan to help artisans continue their work. This approach is helping preserve cultural traditions while boosting tourism. From January to September in 2026, the village received more than 100,000 visitors and generated over 1.85 million yuan in total tourism revenue, said Yan Wenxiang, Party chief of Jinglai Village. Across Yunnan, cultural traditions are closely intertwined with everyday life, as people from different ethnic groups live side by side, share experiences and build bonds while maintaining their customs. Liu Zhen, a guide at the Yunnan Nationalities Museum, knows this firsthand. Born in the 1990s, she grew up in Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture, where different ethnic groups live side by side. For Liu, ethnic diversity was not abstract but part of daily life. Her wardrobe held traditional Yi and Hani clothing, and she joined Jingpo friends in dancing at their festivals. When her legs ached after exercise, her father would take her to a Dai neighbor for herbal remedies. Today, Liu brings that childhood familiarity with different cultures to her work at the museum. She invites visitors to dance to traditional music, experience local festivals and enjoy well-known Dai songs. When visitors ask which ethnic group she belongs to, Liu has a ready answer. "I belong to the Chinese nation, a big family where 56 ethnic groups love and care for each other." ■

item.title: Vietnamese student bridges China and Vietnam through traditional Chinese medicine
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Vietnamese student Lam Quang Duong (L) practices acupuncture under the guidance of his mentor, Dr. Chen Manghua, at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Oct. 21, 2026. Lam enrolled to the university in 2019 and completed his undergraduate studies in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). Now he is pursuing master degree in acupuncture and tuina. Coming from a family of medical professionals, he chose a different path from his family members, most of whom practice Western medicine. His goal was to become the first TCM practitioner in his family. Fluent in Chinese, Lam believes that TCM is not only a medical skill, but also a means of cross-border cultural exchange and heritage preservation. After graduation, he plans to return to Vietnam to practice medicine and continue his clinical and academic work in TCM. "I want to contribute to the medical development of China and Vietnam and help promote the exchange and preservation of traditional medicine between two countries," he said. item.title: A window into 20 years of change along the world's highest railway
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
by Xinhua writer Liu Zhoupeng LHASA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- As a Lhasa-based journalist, I used to see trains simply as transport between assignments. But as the Qinghai-Xizang Railway marked 20 years of operation, the journey itself became my story. In 2006, the Qinghai-Xizang Railway opened to traffic, linking Lhasa, capital of southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, with the rest of the country by rail for the first time. With its highest point at 5,072 meters, it was -- and remains -- the world's highest railway. This time, I bought a ticket to Xining, capital of northwest China's Qinghai Province and the other end of the line, and chose a window seat to see what had changed over 20 years. In the morning, the train pulled out of Lhasa Railway Station. Out the window, glass facades of office buildings caught the sun, and wide boulevards formed a grid across land that had been open fields when the first train departed in 2006. The station is in Liuwu, which became Liuwu New Area a year after the railway opened and is now the Lhasa High-tech Zone, a national-level high-tech zone whose core industries include new energy, the digital economy and financial services. Better access has brought capital, talent and businesses, and local residents have benefited directly. Dawa Sangpo, Party chief of the Liuwu community, whom I met at the ticket gate, said the community operates rental housing, hostels and street shops, and its collective income has increased fivefold. "Six households once received subsistence allowances. Now none do," he told me, adding that per capita annual income has risen from 7,800 yuan (about 1,164 U.S. dollars) to more than 30,000 yuan over the past two decades. The freight has changed too. Train attendant Wang Jiajia, a veteran on this line, told me that early trains carried mostly steel, fuel and daily necessities. Today, freight cars carry household appliances, pet carriers and furniture to the plateau, along with new energy vehicles for export via Xizang. Figures from the railway authorities show that in 2025, freight between the region and the rest of the country increased 22 times over the 2006 level, with outbound shipments such as yak meat and highland barley climbing every year. The railway has become a corridor linking the national market with the plateau's specialty resources, moving more people and goods every year. I was thinking about how the railway had reshaped the plateau when something outside the window caught my eye. As the train rumbled across a modern bridge, the majestic Potala Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage site dating back some 1,300 years, came into view on the hillside, its white walls and gold roofs glowing in the sun. It felt as if history and the present met in a single frame, and for a moment I could hardly look away. The view caused a stir in the carriage. Passengers nudged each other toward the windows, raising phones and cameras to capture the moment. Wang explained that many first-time visitors, both domestic and international, choose to travel to Xizang by train rather than by air. The plateau scenery outside the window is one attraction, and the onboard oxygen supply is another, allowing passengers to adjust gradually to the thin air rather than adapt suddenly after a flight. With its pristine landscapes and rich Tibetan culture, Xizang received over 70.73 million tourist visits in 2025, up 10.71 percent year on year, with total tourism revenue up 9.51 percent to 81.68 billion yuan. Several hours later, the train crested the Tanggula Pass -- the line's highest point at 5,072 meters above sea level -- and pulled into Yanshiping station at 4,721 meters for a four-minute stop. The stop, which opened to passenger service at the end of 2025, serves herders from four townships in Amdo County. I struck up a conversation with Champa, a local herder who boarded at the station. We compared the trip: a bus ride to the county seat could be expensive and took more than four hours. The train now covers the distance in two hours for 30 yuan. As the train rolled north, the view outside shifted from modern buildings to open grassland, where yaks and sheep grazed in the sun. Further on, the vegetation grew sparser, and kiangs and yaks appeared occasionally on the vast plain. The railway has made room for wild animals, with 33 wildlife crossings totaling nearly 60 km located under bridges, on gentle embankment slopes and above tunnels. The 11.7-km Qingshuihe (Clear Water River) Bridge, which also serves as a wildlife corridor across permafrost, and other bridges were raised on stilts, leaving nearly 3,000 openings below. "Trains are not allowed to sound their horns when passing these crossings," Wang told me. Thanks to conservation efforts in recent decades, the number of Tibetan antelopes has increased from over 70,000 in the 1990s to over 300,000, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has adjusted the species' status from endangered to near threatened, reflecting its population recovery. On the human side, the numbers are no less striking. Since it began operation, the Qinghai-Xizang Railway has handled more than 100 million passenger trips, with more than 12.25 million passenger trips in and out of Xizang between 2021 and 2025. Over the years, the rail network in Xizang has grown from a single line into a Y-shaped network, with the Lhasa-Xigaze line opening in 2014 and the Lhasa-Nyingchi line in 2021 joining the original spine. According to a white paper released in March last year, Xizang's operational railway length grew from 701 km in 2012 to 1,359 km in 2024. Inside the carriage, some passengers rested while using supplemental oxygen, some chatted and others looked at their phones. Twenty years ago, boarding a train was an event on the plateau; today it is so ordinary that few people comment on it. I realized the railway has been woven into daily life here, turning the extraordinary into the ordinary. ■

item.title: China-Europe freight train trips top 140,000 as land corridor gains ground
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
A freight train loaded with containers departs from Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Oct. 22, 2026. A China-Europe freight train bound for Moscow departed Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, at around 11:30 a.m. Thursday, bringing the service's cumulative trips to top 140,000 and transporting goods worth over 560 billion U.S. dollars since 2011. Within China, 96 scheduled routes for trains traveling at 120 km per hour link 132 cities along the western, central and eastern corridors, while overseas the network now runs on three lines: northern, central and southern. Together they reach 237 cities in 26 European countries and more than 100 cities in 12 Asian countries, covering most parts of Eurasia, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway), the national rail operator. The southern route is now operating on regular basis, running 746 trains in the first nine months of 2026, up 125 percent year on year. (Xinhua/Pan Yulong) SHENYANG, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The China-Europe freight train service passed 140,000 cumulative trips on Thursday, a milestone that underscores its role as a reliable logistics corridor for Eurasian trade, especially as geopolitical tensions and disruptions to traditional shipping routes challenge global supply chains. The milestone was marked as a train bound for Moscow departed Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, at around 11:30 a.m. Thursday. The value of goods transported by the China-Europe freight train service has exceeded 560 billion U.S. dollars since 2011. The figures reflect that Eurasia's overland corridor has shifted from a niche alternative to a mainstay of regional logistics. This shift is seen not merely in the number of trains, but in what they carry, their destinations, and the reliability of their arrivals. The growth has been steady rather than sudden. Annual trips rose from 1,702 in 2016 to 20,022 in 2025, an average annual increase of more than 30 percent, according to the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC). As a flagship project and a landmark brand of the Belt and Road Initiative, the China-Europe freight train service, also referred to as the "steel camel caravans," has established a comprehensive logistics network across Eurasia. The expansion has come as geopolitical tensions, disruptions to maritime routes and high air freight costs pushed more trade firms to look for stable and efficient transport channels. Rail freight costs roughly one-fifth of air transport and takes about one-quarter of the time of sea transport, and it is less exposed to weather and to disruption on traditional maritime routes, according to the NDRC. The network has broadened in step. Within China, 96 scheduled routes for trains traveling at 120 km per hour link 132 cities along the western, central and eastern corridors, while overseas the network runs on three lines: northern, central and southern. The overseas routes now reach 237 cities in 26 European countries and more than 100 cities in 12 Asian countries, covering most parts of Eurasia, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway), the national rail operator. The southern route shows where that demand is going. Operating on a regular basis, it ran 746 trains in the first nine months of 2026, up 125 percent year on year, far faster than the network as a whole. Regular service linking the Chinese city of Xi'an with Baku, capital of Azerbaijan, began in July 2024, and one such service traverses Central Asia and crosses the Caspian Sea before continuing to Europe either via the overland railway network or by crossing the Black Sea. The reach extends outward as much as inward. Shuai Bin, a professor at the School of Transportation and Logistics at Southwest Jiaotong University, said the service "has drawn global resources and production factors further into inland regions, while fostering a new pattern of opening up featuring highly-coordinated development between coastal ports and inland hubs." On the European side, Duisburg alone handles about 30 percent of China-Europe rail freight volume, according to Markus Teuber, the German city's China affairs commissioner. The range of goods that move along those lines has expanded even faster. Goods now span 53 categories and more than 50,000 items. In the first quarter of 2026, mechanical equipment remained the largest category on outbound trips, followed by automobiles and auto parts. Exports of automobiles and auto parts rose 46 percent year on year, while inbound grains, wood pulp and rubber products climbed 87 percent, 64 percent and 24 percent respectively, data released by China Railway in April showed. According to the operator, the loaded container rate on the return leg had held at 100 percent for 49 consecutive months as of September. "The rising share of return services shows the China-Europe freight trains are shifting from one-way exports to a healthier, two-way trade corridor, helping make Eurasian trade more balanced and sustainable," Sun Zhang, a professor at Tongji University, was quoted by the Global Times as saying. Carrying that cargo reliably is harder than finding it, and reliability rather than speed has now become a primary gauge of the service. Trains running on fixed timetables, with designated numbers, routes and crossing times agreed across borders, cut transit time by about a quarter, and the journey from Xi'an to Duisburg takes as little as 11 days, down from 15. Some 22 such services now link nine Chinese and six European cities, and the average value of a single container is 41 percent higher than on regular trains, according to the NDRC. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for upgrading the service, and the NDRC has said it will improve transport organization, open more alternative routes and deepen coordination with countries along the corridor. An official with the logistics center of China Railway said the operator has been advancing infrastructure connectivity and the alignment of standards and rules to build a smooth, efficient, multi-directional network that connects rails with sea routes. ■ A freight train loaded with containers departs from Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Oct. 22, 2026.(Xinhua/Pan Yulong) Staff members check the conditions of a freight train before its departure at Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Oct. 22, 2026. item.title: "China Haul" reflects growing appeal of shopping in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's commerce ministry said that the "China Haul" trend on overseas social media reflects the rising recognition and appreciation of "Shopping in China." Yang Mu, head of the market operation and consumption promotion department of the Ministry of Commerce, said the phenomenon, depicting foreigners who share their experiences and joy of shopping in China on overseas social platforms, has also been a result of China's high-standard opening up and the charm of fine traditional Chinese culture. While commenting on booming inbound consumption at a press conference on Thursday, Yang said product categories favored by overseas consumers are expanding from traditional specialties such as tea and silk, previously the dominant choices, to tech gadgets, Chinese-style wellness products, beauty products and trendy toys. Shopping has become an important purpose of travel alongside sightseeing for overseas visitors, Yang said, adding that foreign visitors are now visiting more diverse corners of the country in addition to major cities. China continued to attract more foreign visitors in the third quarter of 2026, with visa-free entries rising 24.1 percent year on year to nearly 9 million. Visa-free entries accounted for 77.5 percent of all entries by foreign nationals during the period, official data showed. Building on the country's continued expansion of visa-free arrangements, a series of policy measures have also been rolled out to make shopping in China easier, including upgraded tax refund policies. From January to August this year, nationwide departure tax refund sales increased by about 60 percent year on year, and the number of people receiving tax refunds rose by 300 percent. At present, there are more than 18,000 tax refund stores nationwide, an increase of 400 percent compared with the end of 2024, official data showed. Yang said that going forward, the ministry will work to improve the "Shopping in China" experience by enriching high-quality supply, expanding the coverage of departure tax refunds, and improving payment-related services. ■

item.title: Yangtze River governance shows progress, offers insights for regional cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Along the Yangtze River in Yichang, central China's Hubei Province, steel frames that once supported sand-and-gravel conveyors now hold swings, while a former industrial building has been transformed into an art gallery. The structures stand in Lighthouse Square, a riverside public space created on the site of a former port, where phosphate ore, sand and gravel were once loaded and unloaded. Chen Yuanyuan, a local resident who now volunteers to patrol the riverbank, recalls when dust was so thick that residents kept their windows closed. Today, the restored waterfront has become a popular spot for daily walks and environmental education. Since 2018, Yichang's riverbank restoration project has removed 15 docks, relocated 35 enterprises and 113 households, restored vegetation across 87 hectares and rehabilitated eight kilometers of Yangtze River shoreline. Along the Yangtze River, shoreline restoration is accompanied by broader efforts to improve water quality, control pollution and restore aquatic habitats across the basin. FROM LOCAL RESTORATION TO BASIN-WIDE GOVERNANCE China's efforts to protect the Yangtze River have improved water quality and supported the recovery of native species, although restoring a healthy river ecosystem will require a substantially longer period of time. The Ministry of Ecology and Environment rated the Yangtze River basin's water quality as excellent in the first quarter of 2026. Across the wider Yangtze River Economic Belt, the proportion of monitored sections meeting Grade I to III water quality standards has risen from 67 percent in 2015 to 96.5 percent. Habitat restoration has helped create conditions for the recovery of endangered species. In April 2025, researchers recorded natural spawning and successful hatching of Yangtze sturgeon in a restored spawning ground in the Chishui River, a tributary of the upper Yangtze River. Researchers released 20 adult sturgeon into a restored habitat of about 8,000 square meters, where a natural spawning ground had been created. The species had not reproduced naturally since the early 2000s and was declared extinct in the wild by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2022. The recent successful spawning and hatching mark an important step toward rebuilding a wild population. In 2018, the southwestern Chinese provinces of Yunnan, Guizhou and Sichuan established a water environment compensation fund for the Chishui River basin, creating the first cross-provincial ecological compensation mechanism in the Yangtze River Economic Belt. The three provinces jointly contributed 200 million yuan (about 30 million U.S. dollars) under the initial agreement, with compensation allocations linked to water quality at designated monitoring sections. A second-round agreement signed in 2023 increased annual funding to 300 million yuan for the 2021-2025 period. In the Yunnan section of the Chishui River, water quality at the exit monitoring section had remained at Grade II for five consecutive years as of the end of 2024, while the number of recorded fish species in the section had risen from 36 in early 2020 to 43. At the basin level, the Yangtze River Protection Law, which took effect in March 2021, provides a legal framework for ecological conservation, pollution control and resource management. Under the river chief system, officials at different levels are responsible for waterway protection, with mechanisms in place to clarify responsibilities across administrative boundaries and coordinate action among upstream and downstream areas. According to Li Xiaokai, senior water resources management specialist at the World Bank, China's approach to Yangtze River governance features integrated management of the basin as an ecological and economic system, coordination across government levels and sectors, and the integration of ecological protection with economic development. The World Bank-supported Yangtze River Protection and Ecological Restoration Programs, which cover three provinces in the middle reaches of the river basin, place institutional development at their core, recognizing that sustainable outcomes depend as much on governance systems as on infrastructure investments, said Li. LESSONS FOR REGIONAL COOPERATION Despite differences in geography and development contexts, China and many countries across the Asia-Pacific face similar challenges in river governance and ecological protection, Li said. One major challenge is institutional fragmentation. River basins rarely conform to political boundaries, and responsibilities for water resources, environmental protection, agriculture, energy, transport and land management are often divided among multiple agencies. Decisions made in one sector or jurisdiction can therefore have unintended consequences elsewhere in the basin, said Li. In the Lancang-Mekong basin, China has provided year-round hydrological information from two upstream stations to the Mekong River Commission (MRC) since November 2020, supporting river monitoring and upstream-downstream coordination on flood and drought risks. The country has proposed further cooperation on urgent notifications, wider data sharing across the basin, and joint work on flood forecasting and drought response to strengthen upstream-downstream coordination in addressing flood and drought risks. Sun Jingrui, an associate professor at Yunnan University, said the Yangtze River governance experience shows that fish recovery depends on a governance system capable of sustaining the costs of conservation, rather than on fishing restrictions alone. Fish protection must be treated as both an ecological issue and a matter of food systems and livelihoods, Sun said. Measures to reduce fishing need to be accompanied by alternative sources of income and food, vocational training and social security for affected communities. This is particularly important in the Lancang-Mekong basin, where fish resources are closely linked to food security and community culture, especially in downstream countries. Differences in countries' enforcement capacity, development priorities and dependence on fisheries mean that a uniform, long-term fishing ban across the entire basin would be difficult to implement, Sun said. Fish recovery also requires restoring river connectivity and protecting the habitats needed for fish to complete their life cycles. A paper co-authored by Sun found more than 10,000 small river barriers in the lower Mekong, disrupting connectivity along fish migration routes. Sun suggested introducing seasonal or area-specific fishing restrictions during key migration and breeding periods, prohibiting destructive fishing methods, improving fish passage around barriers and adjusting dam and sluice operations where feasible. Protecting key habitats, including spawning grounds, deep pools and floodplain nursery areas, is another priority, Sun said. "Truly sustainable conservation must give affected people the means to make the transition with dignity," said Sun. ■

item.title: China issues revised administrative measures for outbound investment
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China on Thursday unveiled revised administrative measures for outbound investment, aiming to provide stronger institutional safeguards for its development and security. The measures, released by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), China's top economic planner, will take effect on Dec. 1, 2026, replacing the existing rules enacted in 2017. The revision comes amid rapid growth in China's outbound investment and rising risks in an increasingly complex global environment, a spokesperson for the NDRC said. The revised measures further affirm the principal role of various investors in outbound investment, including domestic enterprises, individual residents, and other organizations. They also improve reporting systems for major adverse events and large overseas reinvestment projects, aiming to better protect the rights and interests of outbound investors and help them manage overseas risks. The revision is part of the country's broader efforts to promote the high-quality development of outbound investment. In June, China issued a new regulation on outbound investment, which calls for proactively aligning with high-standard international economic and trade rules, advancing high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, and promoting international cooperation in industrial and supply chains. China's outbound investment has continued to expand in recent years. By the end of 2025, the country's outbound investment stock had reached nearly 3.4 trillion U.S. dollars, keeping China among the world's top three investors for nine consecutive years, according to the Ministry of Commerce. The ministry also reported that China's outbound direct investment maintained steady and orderly growth, totaling 128.62 billion U.S. dollars in the first three quarters of 2026. ■

item.title: China's top legislature to review draft law on Antarctic activities, environmental protection
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Zhao Leji, chairman of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, presides over the 74th meeting of the Council of Chairpersons of the 14th NPC Standing Committee at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Weibing) BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislature will deliberate on the draft law on Antarctic activities and environmental protection during its upcoming session, marking the third review of the draft law. The enactment of the law was listed on the legislative plan of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee for 2026. The previous two reviews took place in December 2025 and June this year, respectively. The 14th NPC Standing Committee will hold its 25th session from Nov. 2 to 6, according to a Thursday meeting of the Council of Chairpersons of the standing committee presided over by NPC Standing Committee Chairman Zhao Leji. Apart from the draft law on Antarctic affairs, lawmakers at the session will review draft laws on public interest litigation by procuratorates, state-owned assets and finance, a draft law against cross-border corruption, and a draft revision to the Water Law. They will review bills for deliberation on a draft amendment to the Criminal Procedure Law, and draft revisions to the Renewable Energy Law and the Tax Collection Administration Law, among other draft amendments. A bill for deliberation on the ratification of the agreement on establishing the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization will also be reviewed at the session. ■

item.title: Xi calls for new achievements on new Long March
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Yao Dawei) BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for new achievements on the new Long March as China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March. "Only by remembering history can we create a brighter future," said Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, when addressing a gathering held in Beijing to mark the anniversary. Under Xi's proposal, all participants stood up and observed a moment of silence for the revolutionary heroes who gave their lives during the Long March and in revolutionary struggles across China. From October 1934 to October 1936, the Red Army marched through more than 10 provinces during the Long March, opening up a new chapter in the Chinese revolution, Xi said. "This earth-shattering revolutionary feat holds great significance in the history of our Party, country and military, and has a profound impact on our path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," he noted. Xi stressed that the Party's right leadership and the establishment of Mao Zedong's core position were decisive for the victory of the Red Army's Long March. The Party and the Red Army relied on firm conviction, Xi said, adding that troops with noble ideals and firm beliefs are invincible. Xi emphasized the importance of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities in addressing the country's issues and problems. He further underscored that the people will always be the source of strength and a strong support for the Party and the people's armed forces. Xi said the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. "It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously." He said the road of the Long March continues to extend. "On our new journey, we are now committed to realizing the Second Centenary Goal of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through a Chinese path to modernization," he said. To forge ahead on the new Long March, Xi said, it is imperative to stay committed to the Party's ideals, convictions and purpose and rely closely on the people to create new achievements. He underscored the need to unswervingly advance high-quality development and promote common prosperity for all. Efforts must be made to better ensure both development and security and seize the historical initiative to overcome difficulties, combat risks and meet challenges, he stressed. Xi also emphasized the importance of moving more quickly to reinforce the people's armed forces to world-class standards and adhering to the Party's absolute leadership over the military. It is also vital to uphold the leadership of the Party, strengthen Party building and persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance, he added. Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi, who are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, as well as Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, attended the gathering. Zhao, who presided over the event, said Xi's speech was of immense political, ideological and guiding significance, urging earnest efforts to study and grasp its essence and ensure its effective implementation. He called on the whole Party, the entire military and the Chinese people of all ethnic groups to rally more closely around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core and strive to build a great country and advance national rejuvenation on all fronts through Chinese modernization.
